comparator.name: International Bachelor History
comparator.route: Economic History focus area with minor and internship
comparator.sourceNotes: Current 2026–2027 ESHCC TER Appendix 9 establishes the exact 21-component 180-EC History/IBH pathway; Appendix 6 establishes its historical and social-science inquiry and four focus areas. The English full-time IBH target is distinct from the Dutch-language offering. The public overview contains older first-year labels and descriptions; these do not replace the current formal component names or establish unchanged assignments. Four focus areas are equally specialised; Economic History is first in the current formal table and is the neutral tie-break, independently of UCR fit. Option 1 and its first-listed internship instantiate the third-year choices. Articles 3.5–3.7, 4.3–4.5, 9.2 and A11.2 govern attendance, choices, progression and thesis conditions.
components: Historical Identities in a Changing World Order
Philosophy of History in a Globalizing World
One permitted 7.5-EC elective; options are listed by the programme. No particular unverified elective is invented.
Thesis class in the Economic History focus area. Entry requires completed BA1 and 45 EC in BA2/3, including 22.5 EC in the focus area (three courses).

Individually assessed historical research within the selected focus-area thesis class. The class must be completed before submission. A timely submitted thesis has a resit under the TER; the resit grade is capped at 6.0.

One 15-EC minor from the admission matrix, with its admission requirements; participation requires at least third-year enrolment. The selected route does not combine this with the alternative exchange or educational-minor route.

Selected 15-EC field-specific placement, replaceable by two permitted electives. Entry requires all BA1 courses passed. Normally in the second term of Year 3 for History; another term may be requested. Approved placement concludes within six consecutive months and is graded pass/fail.

routeSelection.route: Economic History focus area with minor and internship
routeSelection.basis: The generic English-language IBH target does not choose a focus area. The four areas are equally specialised and none is established as the broad default; Economic History is first in the current formal TER Appendix 9. Option 1 (minor, public-role course and internship or two electives) is first; internship is first within that choice. Use those formal orders as neutral tie-breaks before UCR selection.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Modern and global history since 1300 in long-term perspective
Historical explanation of contemporary politics, economics, culture and social relations
Migration, identity, inequality, colonialism and belonging across history
Primary-source research, quantitative and qualitative historical methods, historiography and academic writing
Economic history, capitalism, labour, business, states and international economic relations
Independent historical research and the public role of historians
adjacent: International relations, conflict, global power and political institutions in historical perspective
Social history, social theory, migration, inequality and collective change
Cultural history, ideas, representation, heritage and collective memory
Dutch and colonial history in global context
questions: How do long-term historical developments explain present political, economic, social and cultural challenges?
How can historical sources, data, historiography and representation be analysed critically?
How have empire, migration, conflict, inequality and identity shaped global societies?

trace: develops critical source use, academic communication, ethical reflection and professional engagement

candidates.label: International relations, conflict and global power

selection.assessment: Three concepts survive sequential evidence, comparability, distinctness and feasibility review. The closest response combines direct historical inquiry with economic/social explanation and strengthened historiography. The second changes the governing question to international order and conflict; the third to social experience and cultural evidence. Each retains substantial actual historical subject study and primary-source inquiry; none rests solely on generic complementary courses or a disclaimer. The four formal external focus areas support the candidates; no fourth option is authorised or needed.

alternatives.label: History, economy & society
alternatives.labelReason: All six History courses provide the historical core. Economics and social theory explain economic/social change; art history and historiography add interpretation of cultural evidence. Contemporary economics complements historical inquiry rather than substituting for specialist Economic History.
alternatives.concept: Modern history, empire, warfare, gender and Indigenous histories form the core. Economics and sociology support analysis of economic and social change, while art history, historiography, qualitative and quantitative methods, primary-source research and rhetoric develop interpretation and communication.
progression: Modern History, economics and sociology begin in Semester 1. Research Methods & Statistics precedes the selected economics courses that require it; qualitative methodology precedes later empirical analysis. Modern Sociology precedes advanced social theory. Western Art History in Semester 5 precedes Writing Art’s Histories in Semester 6; the final History Research Seminar examines primary sources on the 1809 Walcheren Expedition. Rhetoric precedes its community-engagement continuation. These advisory sequences supplement, rather than add to, the formal prerequisites and planned offerings.

alternatives.label: History, international relations & conflict
alternatives.labelReason: The route retains all six UCR History courses while concentrating its adjacent work in comparative politics, international relations, conflict, international and EU law, institutions and global governance. The label states the organising fields without claiming a dedicated diplomatic-history degree.
alternatives.concept: Modern history, empires, Western warfare, gender and Indigenous histories are studied alongside international-relations theory, political thought, comparative politics, conflict and peace, human rights and legal institutions. Sociology, qualitative research and public rhetoric support historically informed analysis of power and international order.
alternatives.distinctness: This option differs from the closest programme by 8 courses (60 EC) per programme. Its governing priority is international order, institutions, conflict and power: political/legal analysis replaces the economics strand and art-historical interpretation while retaining the six-course History core. Contemporary law supports historically informed inquiry but is not itself diplomatic history.
progression: Modern History, Law, Society & Justice and comparative politics begin in Semester 1. The law gateway precedes the later law courses that require it. International-relations theory precedes Peace & Conflict, and Modern Sociology precedes advanced social theory. Qualitative methodology occurs in the final semester and supplies complementary social research methods; it is not a prerequisite for the History Research Seminar. The final seminar concerns primary sources from the 1809 Walcheren Expedition, rather than a freely chosen international-relations thesis. Rhetoric precedes its practical continuation.

alternatives.label: Social & cultural history
alternatives.labelReason: The route retains the complete available UCR History sequence and adds sociology, gender, movements, art and heritage, archaeology, literature, museums, race, documentary and historical writing. The label follows the coherent overlap of the comparator's Social and Cultural History focus areas.
alternatives.concept: Historical inquiry into societies and cultural expression combines all six History courses with sociology, social movements, art and material culture, archaeology, heritage, museums, literature, film, race and documentary. Historical and art-historical research, qualitative methods and public rhetoric support analysis of evidence, representation and memory.
alternatives.distinctness: This option differs from the closest programme by 9 courses (67.5 EC) per programme. Its governing priority is historical experience, representation and cultural evidence: art, heritage, archaeology, literature, media and social movements replace economic and political analysis. These content changes implement the combined Social/Cultural History direction. It also differs from the international-relations option by 11 courses per programme.
progression: Modern History, sociology and Western Art History begin in Semester 1; introductory literary interpretation precedes Film & Text. Modern Sociology precedes advanced social theory; art and heritage courses precede the historiography of art in the final semester. Qualitative methodology precedes the final History Research Seminar. World Archaeology is taken in Year 2 because of its offering and adds ancient material-culture methods; the programme does not imply a separate foundation prerequisite. Rhetoric precedes its community-engagement continuation. All formal prerequisites and assigned offerings are checked separately.

blocks: Both survey modern political, economic and cultural change across a broad chronological and international frame; UCR begins in 1815 rather than 1500.
Both compare societies through global encounters and unequal power; UCR ranges across empires more broadly and is not confined to 1300-1800.
The external modern-societies survey is not reproduced by a separate UCR course; UCR’s broad Modern History course is already shown with Global History.
Both analyse colonialism, identity, belonging and changing historical orders; UCR concentrates on Native American histories.

Partial research relationship: UCR investigates primary sources on the 1809 Walcheren Expedition and writes a substantial paper. The external class prepares a separate thesis in the chosen Economic History focus area.

The UCR History Research Seminar develops historical research at advanced level but is already aligned to the comparator's focus-area thesis class; UCR has no separate introductory Becoming a Historian course.
UCR courses repeatedly connect past and present, but there is no separate historiography-and-contemporary-relevance course matching Rethinking History.
UCR offers philosophy courses, but none of the scheduled courses is a dedicated philosophy-of-history course.
The comparator requires a 15-EC individual History thesis. None of the 24 scheduled UCR courses is a thesis, so UCR's optional independent-research element is displayed alongside it.
The comparator component is an open History elective, while UCR elective choice is distributed throughout each 180-EC pathway; no single scheduled course is asserted as its equivalent.
Research methods, writing & the public role of history
Both teach research design and statistical analysis; the comparator applies those methods specifically to historical data.
Both teach systematic qualitative collection and interpretation; the comparator specialises in historical sources and techniques such as discourse, narrative and oral-history analysis.

Partial skill relationship in academic argument, essay structure and speaking. UCR teaches general rhetoric; the external component is specifically historical writing. No unchanged word-count requirement is assumed from older overview copy.
UCR has public rhetoric and civic formation, but no scheduled course specifically trains the public role of historians.
The comparator's 15-EC minor is an open external-field choice. UCR breadth is distributed across the full liberal-arts curriculum, so no one scheduled course is treated as the minor.
The selected comparator route requires a 15-EC field-specific internship. None of the scheduled UCR courses is an internship or equivalent workplace placement.

Partial relationship in international economic processes and trade. UCR teaches macroeconomic theory and policy; the external course studies economic globalisation and international power historically.
No selected UCR course establishes historical multinational–state relations.
The dedicated historical inquiry into emerging economies and global labour has no adequate selected-course correspondence.
Partial relationship in inequality, institutions and redistribution. UCR uses contemporary economic theory and evidence; the external component investigates capitalism and inequality historically.
Both introduce sociological concepts and theories as tools for understanding societies; the comparator applies them explicitly in historical research.

notes.text: Erasmus provides a continuous History degree, specialist historical methods and philosophy, a chosen focus area, thesis preparation and a required individual History thesis. Each UCR option contains six History courses, including primary-source research, with different economic, political or cultural combinations. UCR does not reproduce the complete specialist sequence, the required thesis or the selected internship. Its economics, law and rhetoric courses are complementary contributions with distinct aims.

audience.programmeDescription: The English-taught International Bachelor History at Erasmus University Rotterdam studies global historical change and uses historical and social-science methods to investigate contemporary questions. Students choose a focus area and complete an individual History thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR option combines historical inquiry with economic and social explanation. The second focuses on international relations, conflict and institutions; the third on social and cultural history. Each includes all six UCR History courses and a primary-source research seminar. Economics, law, rhetoric and other fields support those historical questions while retaining their own methods. Shared rows show partial subject or skill relationships; blank cells preserve substantive gaps.
